paras: The lynching of Frank Livingston was the killing of a Black farm hand and recently discharged soldier who was tied to a tree and burned to death by a mob near Eldorado, Union County, Arkansas, on May 21, 1919. He had been accused of killing his white employer and the employer's wife after a quarrel. No arrests were reported, and the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People protested to Governor Charles Brough, calling it the second lynching in Arkansas within thirty days.

According to an Eldorado dispatch in the Chicago Defender, Livingston was a farm hand and "a returned soldier" who quarreled with Clay Robinson, a white man, over the distribution of chickens. The Defender's account says Robinson fired on Livingston, who then took an ax and felled him, and that Robinson's wife seized the gun and turned it on Livingston. The Defender stated that Livingston killed both Robinsons, while the NAACP described him only as "accused of murdering his employer and the latter's wife following a quarrel."

Livingston was taken from his home by what the Defender called "a crowd of unmasked white men" and tied to a tree about 18 miles from Eldorado. The Defender reported that his body was hacked with butcher knives and glass bottles before it was burned, and that he was burned alive. Press dispatches cited by the NAACP said Sheriff Craig of Union County arrived a few minutes too late to prevent the lynching, whereas the Defender said the police arrived but made no attempt to intervene.

No arrests were made, according to the press dispatches the NAACP relayed. On May 23 the NAACP, through its secretary John R. Shillady, telegraphed Governor Brough asking what steps Arkansas authorities were taking against the lynchers, noting that Arkansas law provided "ample punishment" for murder. The telegram reminded Brough of his leadership of the Southern Sociological Congress, which had just passed resolutions against lynching, and urged him to act "as a man, no less than as governor."
In its May 30 dispatch, the Defender's correspondent wrote that nothing had been done to bring the guilty parties to justice and that people were leaving the area.

The case reached the Black press on May 31, 1919, chiefly through the NAACP's protest, which the Colorado Statesman, the Dallas Express and the Savannah Tribune printed with the full text of the telegram. The reprints varied in their accuracy: the Savannah Tribune placed the burning "near Colorado, Ark.," and the Dallas Express's Associated Negro Press version printed the place as Elkton, Maryland. The Savannah Tribune headlined the release as a protest "against the burning of a Negro."

The Chicago Defender ran its own dispatch the same day under the headline "Arkansas Mob Burns," the only account with details of the quarrel and the mutilation, and it closed by noting that Livingston was a returned soldier. The New York Age, reprinting a New York World editorial on pogroms in Europe, alluded to Negroes lynched and burned in Arkansas and Mississippi a few days earlier without naming them. In July the Richmond Planet, quoting The Sun, listed the burning among the year's "illegal executions of Negroes" carried out despite President Wilson's appeal against mob rule.

The NAACP release and the Planet date the lynching May 21, but the Defender's May 30 dispatch says "last Wednesday," which would be May 28; the NAACP telegram, dated May 23, supports the earlier date. Accounts of the mob also differ: the Defender described unmasked white men, while the Planet described a mob of 150 "whites and Negroes."

accounts.label: Eldorado dispatch (Chicago Defender)
accounts.gist: Livingston killed Clay Robinson and his wife after Robinson fired on him in an argument over chickens; a crowd of unmasked white men took him from home, hacked his body and burned him alive while police did not intervene.

accounts.label: NAACP telegram, citing press dispatches
accounts.gist: Livingston, accused of murdering his employer and the employer's wife after a quarrel, was tied to a tree and burned by a mob near Eldorado on May 21; Sheriff Craig arrived too late and no arrests were made.

accounts.label: Richmond Planet list (quoting The Sun)
accounts.gist: On May 21 Livingston was tied to a tree and burned to death by a mob of 150 whites and Negroes at El Dorado.

framing.detail: The Defender headlined 'Arkansas Mob Burns', noted Livingston was 'a returned soldier' and that nothing had been done to punish the 'guilty parties'.
The Colorado Statesman, Dallas Express and Savannah Tribune ran the NAACP protest, which called the lynching a 'barbarity' and stressed Arkansas law gave 'ample punishment' for murder.
The Richmond Planet placed it in a list of 1919 burnings it called 'illegal executions of Negroes' defying President Wilson's appeal against mob rule.

conflicts.note: The NAACP telegram is dated May 23, before May 28, so the May 21 date is better supported.
The Defender's dispatch is from Eldorado; the Planet's later list does not give its source beyond The Sun.

conflicts.note: The NAACP relayed press dispatches; the Defender's wording (OCR-damaged) implies officers were present during the lynching.
